title: Partial differential equations predominate largely by historical accident

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Partial differential equations predominate largely by historical accident

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The dominance of partial differential equations as models in science is in many respects a historical accident of their being solvable by explicit formulas before computers; had computers come earlier, scientific modeling would probably be very different.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: I suspect that in fact the current predominance of partial differential equations is in many respects a historical accident—and that had computer technology been developed earlier in the history of mathematics, the situation would probably now be very different.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 4, “Systems Based on Numbers”; section “Partial Differential Equations” (from p. 161), p. 162. Scope: history of mathematical modeling in physics and other sciences

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch04-24: not-empirically-resolvable, resolvability 0.33

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Public literature metadata can document changing modeling practices but cannot confirm or refute the stated alternate history. Any causal conclusion would depend on strong, untestable assumptions rather than discriminating existing data.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Bibliometric and historical records could measure correlations between analytic solvability, computer availability, and model adoption. They cannot observe the counterfactual history in which computers arrived earlier or identify historical accident independently of competing social causes.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Technological timing is confounded with mathematical, experimental, and institutional developments.

Historical accident has no unique decision criterion.

The central claim is an unobservable historical counterfactual.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Wolfram offers a suspicion about why partial differential equations came to dominate, based on their solvability before computers. That is a counterfactual historical judgment. Archives of mathematics can support a narrative about actual motives; they do not contain the world in which computers arrived earlier, so the claim has no confirming or refuting observation.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: The claim is a counterfactual: had computers arrived earlier in the history of mathematics, scientific models would probably not be dominated by partial differential equations. Historical sources can document why those equations were used; they cannot instantiate the other timeline.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
'In many respects a historical accident' can be retained or withdrawn without a change in any dataset.

A counterfactual history has no observable that would confirm or refute it.
